segments.spokenText: Part 4. Why museum stores need good information. You now have one minute to read questions 31 to 40.

A museum store is often imagined as a room full of objects waiting to appear in an exhibition. In practice, it is an information system with physical responsibilities. An object that is preserved perfectly but cannot be found is unavailable for research. An object that can be found but has lost its identity may be equally difficult to interpret. Today we'll follow the basic journey of an item entering a fictional local museum, concentrating on the connection between its physical location and its documentary record.

Today we’ll follow the basic journey of an item entering a fictional local museum, concentrating on the connection between its physical location and its documentary record.

segments.spokenText: The museum first establishes ownership. A donation, a loan and an item left temporarily for identification create different obligations. Staff should not assume that possession means permission to display, alter or dispose of an object. The agreement records what has been transferred and which conditions apply. This may sound administrative, but uncertainty here can undermine later decisions, especially when the person who brought the item is no longer available to explain the original conversation. A clear record protects the museum and the people connected with the object.

segments.spokenText: Each accepted object receives a unique number. That number links the item to its catalogue record, photographs and associated documents. It should not depend on a shelf location, because objects move. A label that says only where an item currently sits becomes misleading when a store is rearranged. Staff use an appropriate marking method that does not damage the material, and detachable parts need a documented relationship to the whole. Otherwise a lid and a container can become two apparently unrelated mysteries after being separated for treatment.

segments.spokenText: A condition report describes the object's state at entry. It distinguishes existing damage from changes observed later. Good photographs help, but a photograph alone may not show a loose joint, an unstable surface or a part hidden from view. Staff combine images with written observations and specify which areas could not be inspected. The report should not make an uncertain diagnosis sound definitive. A mark that might be mould requires investigation and precaution, not a confident label added by someone without the relevant expertise.

segments.spokenText: Storage supports are chosen for the item, rather than forcing every object into identical packaging. A heavy piece may need support across its base; a fragile projection may need space around it. The support should allow safe handling without unnecessary direct contact. Where practical, a tray can move with the object. Shelving must also accommodate retrieval, since packing objects densely can make access hazardous. The apparent efficiency of filling every gap disappears if retrieving one item requires moving several vulnerable neighbours.

segments.spokenText: Location records must change whenever an object moves. This includes temporary moves to photography, conservation or an educational session, not just permanent transfers between stores. The record identifies who moved it, when and where it is expected to be. A temporary location left undocumented can become a long-term disappearance. Staff therefore check movements as part of ordinary work rather than waiting for an annual inventory to reveal that something is missing. Regular audits test whether the system describes what is actually on the shelves.

segments.spokenText: The catalogue also contains interpretation: what an object may have been used for, who made it and which evidence supports those claims. New research can revise these accounts. The system should retain a history of changes instead of silently replacing an earlier attribution. A researcher may need to understand why an object was once described differently. Separating observation from interpretation helps too. Dimensions measured directly have a different status from a maker's name inferred from a resemblance, even when both appear in the same database entry.

segments.spokenText: Finally, digital records need their own care. Backups should be tested, and access permissions should protect sensitive information without making routine work impossible. A copy that has never been restored offers uncertain protection. The museum also needs a plan for future software changes so that records remain usable when a particular application becomes obsolete. Caring for a collection means caring for the connections that make objects meaningful. The physical store and the catalogue are partners: neither can fulfil the museum's responsibility while the other is neglected.
